abstract: Lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is one pathological aspect of retinal degenerative disorders, which contribute to the buildup of autofluorescent undegraded materials such as lipofuscin. A comprehensive understanding of lipofuscin biology remains a critical gap in the field. Here, we explore the cell biology of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules (AFGs) within RPE cells and the potential of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) activation to promote its clearance in human RPE cells. Under steady-state conditions we find that photoreceptor outer segments (POS) phagocytosis by the RPE is sufficient to trigger NRF2 activation, suggesting a feedback mechanism that links phagocytic activity with cytoprotective stress responses. RPE fed with excess POS accumulate lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules (AFG) within hours, a measure of lysosomal dysfunction. These AFGs gradually loose connection with the endocytic system and remain as ''storage granules'' within RPE. Pre-treatment or delayed pharmacological activation of NRF2 with dimethyl fumarate (DMF) significantly decrease accumulation of AFGs, suggesting improved clearance mechanisms. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of autophagy totally abolish these effects. Similarly, compromised autophagy also abolished the clearance effects observed with inhibition of the mTOR pathway. Collectively, these results suggest a 3-step lipofuscin cycle within the RPE (formation, storage and clearance), provide mechanistic evidence that autophagy is an essential process for the clearance of AFGs and that NRF2-activation and other stimulators of autophagy may represent novel therapeutic strategies to restore RPE homeostasis and mitigate retinal degeneration.
